title: Lithium Overload Reveals a Sun-Like Star's Planetary Meal
summary:
Astronomers have uncovered compelling evidence that a sun-like star 1,300 light-years away consumed one of its own planets. The star, TOI-5882, exhibits an abnormally high abundance of lithium—a telltale sign of planetary engulfment. "You are what you eat," said lead author Brooke Kotten, a graduate researcher at the University of Michigan. "We know that there's much more lithium in planetary material than there is in stars. So if a star eats a planet, it's going to take on a bunch of lithium."

The team, which included 14 researchers from the U.S. and Chile, used spectroscopy to analyze TOI-5882's light. They found lithium levels far exceeding what's typical for a star of its type. Based on the amount, they estimate the swallowed planet was between a couple of Earth masses and the mass of Neptune. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, mark a significant step in identifying such events, which are fleeting on cosmic timescales—lasting only days or weeks—and rarely caught in the act.

But how did the planet end up as a stellar snack? TOI-5882 hasn't yet expanded into a red giant, so size alone can't explain it. The culprit may be a brown dwarf orbiting the star: an object more than 20 times Jupiter's mass but too small to ignite nuclear fusion. Its gravitational influence could have destabilized the planet's orbit, sending it on a death spiral. This scenario will be investigated in a separate study.

The research has implications for our own solar system. In roughly 5 billion years, the sun will swell into a red giant and likely engulf Mercury, Venus, and possibly Earth. "The fact that we can look at a star 1,300 light-years away and say with confidence, 'This star has more lithium than you would expect,' is a testament to both the precision of modern instrumentation and the hard interpretive work that goes into making sense of that signal," said Melinda Soares-Furtado, a senior author and assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin. By learning to read these chemical fingerprints, astronomers hope to piece together how often planets meet this fiery end—and what it means for the evolution of planetary systems.
why_it_matters: Studying stars that swallowed planets reveals the violent future that may await our own Earth and teaches us about the dynamic life cycles of planetary systems, helping us understand our place in the cosmos.

background_read: Stars like our Sun can swallow their planets under certain conditions. When a star exhausts its nuclear fuel and expands into a red giant—a late, bloated phase—its outer layers may engulf close-in worlds. In about 5 billion years, the Sun will become a red giant and likely consume Mercury, Venus, and possibly Earth. However, planets can also be ingested much earlier if gravitational tugs from a companion object disturb their orbits. A brown dwarf (a 'failed star' with a mass between that of a giant planet and a small star) can send a planet spiraling inward. This is not the first detection of planetary engulfment: in 2017, a star nicknamed Kronos was found with an unusually high level of heavy elements, likely from a swallowed planet. Lithium is a key tracer because it is easily destroyed inside stars but survives in planets. An excess of lithium therefore strongly suggests the star recently ate planetary material.

The TESS satellite (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) first identified TOI-5882 as interesting, and ground-based spectroscopy measured the lithium abundance. This chemical fingerprint allows astronomers to study how often planets end up as stellar meals, giving a glimpse of a fate that may one day befall our own world.

perspectives.description: This discovery gives astronomers a new and reliable tool—lithium fingerprinting—to identify planetary engulfment events, even long after they happen. It opens the door to building a census of such events across the galaxy.

The method relies on a single chemical element, so false positives are possible if the star gained lithium from another source, such as a close binary interaction. More evidence is needed before every lithium-rich star can be labeled a planet-eater.

Stars swallowing planets is part of normal stellar evolution. Studying these events reveals the chaotic gravitational interactions that shape planetary systems, showing that stable systems like ours may be the exception rather than the rule.

Upcoming large-scale surveys by telescopes like the Vera Rubin Observatory could find hundreds of stars with similar lithium signatures. That statistical sample will let astronomers estimate how often planets perish this way and refine predictions for our own solar system’s future.
